questions.q: What is a classification in Microsoft Purview?
options: A logical tag describing the kind of data an asset contains, based on its business context
A permission level granted to a user
The name of the collection an asset belongs to
A billing tier for the Data Map
questions.explain: A classification is a logical tag — like Passport Number, Credit Card Number, or Person's Name — assigned to an asset based on the actual business context of the data it contains.

questions.q: What does the thunderbolt icon next to a classification name indicate?
options: The classification failed to apply
It's a system classification, one of Purview's 200+ built-in classifications
The asset has been deleted
The classification was applied by a different Purview account
questions.explain: The thunderbolt icon marks a classification as a system classification — one of the 200+ built-in classifications Purview ships with, as opposed to a custom one you created yourself.

questions.q: Besides automatic classification during a scan, how else can a classification be applied to an asset?
options: Classifications can never be changed once applied
Only Microsoft support can add classifications
Manually, through the asset's own detail page by selecting Edit
Only by deleting and re-registering the source
questions.explain: In addition to automatic classification during a scan, you can manually add classifications on an asset's Overview tab any time afterward, by selecting Edit and choosing from the Classifications dropdown.

questions.q: Can a system classification and a custom classification be applied to the same asset at the same time?
options: No, an asset can only have one type of classification
Yes — mixing a system classification with a custom one on the same asset is completely normal
Only if the custom classification is deleted first
Only for table assets, never for files
questions.explain: An asset can carry both system and custom classifications simultaneously — for example, a system classification like Credit Card Number alongside a custom one like CustomerAccountID.

questions.q: Why don't table assets get classifications applied automatically during a scan, unlike files and columns?
options: Because classifications live on the table's columns, not the table asset itself
Because table assets are never scanned at all
Because tables don't support classifications under any circumstances
Because only Azure SQL Database supports table classification
questions.explain: Scanning automatically classifies file and column assets, but not table assets, because classifications are assigned at the column level — to show a classification on the table asset itself, you have to add it manually.
